overview.title:
BECOMING
DOOM
overview.subtitle: A life you can stand behind
overview.notes: Introduce the course as structured practice in agency, judgement and sustained action. The working promise is to stop asking unnecessary permission to build a chosen life and develop the will, judgement and capability to act. Do not promise invulnerability, income or an already validated transformation. Source: PROJECT_CHARTER.md.

overview.title:
Your life deserves
your investment
overview.body: Selfishness as a virtue means deliberate responsibility for your own flourishing.
overview.caption: Choices carry consequences. Commitments still matter.
overview.notes: Ask participants to name a meaningful priority that keeps losing time to less important demands. Explain self-interest as a long-term practice that includes chosen responsibilities, relationships and fair exchange. Indomitable will means purposeful persistence with the ability to revise methods when reality changes. Confidence is not proof. Source: PROJECT_CHARTER.md; curriculum/PRINCIPLES.md P01, P06.

overview.title: Six core stages
rows: A chosen priority and a personal doctrine
An operating system you can trust
A demonstrated skill and a working prototype
Useful work tested with its intended audience
A demonstration, an evidence dossier and a continuation plan
overview.notes: These are six teaching stages. Each builds on the previous stage. Throne: whose life am I building? Fortress: can I trust my execution? Laboratory: what can I now do? Room: can I hold my ground? Empire: will anyone use this? Doomsday: does it hold together? Continue to practise agency and boundaries throughout. Source: curriculum/ARCHITECTURE.md; curriculum/weeks/01.md through 06.md.

overview.title: Four territories
rows: Readiness and recovery, adapted to your circumstances
overview.notes: Command applies throughout. Body supports sustained action and requires individual adaptation rather than a universal training prescription. Capability becomes explicit in the Laboratory. Empire connects capability to work that another person can use. Physical ability, income or charisma do not determine human worth or course completion. Source: curriculum/ARCHITECTURE.md; PROJECT_CHARTER.md.

overview.title: One Doom Project
overview.body: A useful deliverable for a real audience, within the time and resources you have.
overview.caption: Name the audience. Define the evidence. Take the first step.
overview.notes: The project is the action component of the course, not a second workload. Ask: who is it for, what useful thing will exist, how will we tell it works, and what is feasible within available time? Examples may include a portfolio, a service prototype or an internal improvement. Adapt project scope with the facilitator. Show an early version to the intended audience and revise it from actual responses. Source: curriculum/weeks/01.md W01-D05; curriculum/ARCHITECTURE.md.

overview.title: The DOOM method
rows: Choose the priority and the trade-off
Complete the agreed work with appropriate effort
Review the evidence, recover and adjust
overview.notes: The four method names are settled founder direction. The explanatory lines are concise teaching interpretations. Outwork means purposeful execution, not sleep deprivation or indiscriminate hours. Maintain includes recovery and intelligent revision. Ask learners to locate a recent failure: unclear decision, poor setup, insufficient execution or absent review? Source: PROJECT_CHARTER.md; curriculum/ARCHITECTURE.md.

overview.title: The creed
overview.subtitle: PRINCIPLES 01–07
items: Accept that there is no inherent meaning
Hold a vision and be ruthless
overview.notes: Preserve these founder-supplied headings while teaching their definitions explicitly. P01: prioritise flourishing while considering responsibilities. P02: chosen meaning is a philosophical position, not an established fact or a requirement to abandon religion. P03: decisiveness without intimidation. P04: exacting focus that remains open to evidence. P05: useful assets and fair exchange. P06: capacity to act and learn, not certainty of correctness. P07: sustained practice with feedback, not a claim of mastery after this programme. Source: curriculum/PRINCIPLES.md.

overview.title: The creed
overview.subtitle: PRINCIPLES 08–14
items: Master the art of the tactical withdrawal
Treat your body as the ultimate weapon
Despise comfort and seek the friction
overview.notes: P08 releases unnecessary reassurance-seeking, not consent or real authorisation. P09 concerns controllable responses, not blame for illness, disadvantage or others' actions. P10 creates useful responses to disruption without exploiting distress. P11 sets reasons to change or withdraw without avoiding every difficulty. P12 supports appropriate readiness and recovery. P13 uses purposeful, proportionate discomfort rather than treating suffering as proof. P14 uses finite time to choose and exclude. Source: curriculum/PRINCIPLES.md.

overview.title: A reasoning toolkit
overview.caption: Choose a tool because it helps the decision.
overview.notes: Introduce two tools per stage from Fortress onward and reuse previous tools. The toolkit mixes concepts and practical heuristics, not ten universal scientific laws. State an assumption and an action. Opportunity cost needs realistic alternatives. Inferred incentives are not facts. Probability numbers need a basis. Buffers cost resources. First principles does not justify dismissing expertise. Source: curriculum/MENTAL_MODELS.md.

overview.title: The daily record
rows: What did I choose and do?
overview.notes: Keep the record brief. Recall older learning without notes, complete a useful action and review the result. From Fortress onward, note which available reasoning tool helped or why none was needed. A considered yes, a renegotiated agreement or an honoured commitment can show agency. A no is not required each day. Source: curriculum/ARCHITECTURE.md.

overview.title: The evidence of completion
rows: A chosen direction and a workable project scope
Execution, boundaries and honest recovery records
A demonstrated skill and a checked reusable aid
Useful work tested with people who could use it
A defended decision and a ninety-day plan
overview.notes: Assess six dimensions: agency and self-interest, boundaries and commitments, judgement, execution and recovery, capability and value, adaptation. Use demonstrated, revise or not yet evidenced. Give a specific revision request and permit resubmission. Evidence can remain private or redacted. Another person's praise, purchase or agreement is not the grade. Source: curriculum/ASSESSMENT.md.

overview.title:
What will you
stand behind?
overview.body:
Choose one priority worth protecting.
Give it a concrete next action.
overview.notes: Invite a private written answer. Ask each participant to name what the priority requires and what they will stop doing to make room. Explain that the Council provides rehearsal, demonstrations and useful feedback. A setback is information. Notice, record, repair and resume. Source: curriculum/ARCHITECTURE.md; PROJECT_CHARTER.md.

lesson.title:
THE
FIRST NO
lesson.subtitle: The courage to be disliked
lesson.notes: 0:00–1:00. Think about the last time you said yes while hoping the other person would withdraw the request. Perhaps you were busy, or had finally found an hour for something important. You agreed anyway, then felt irritated with them for asking. Return to the moment before you agreed. What did you want to protect? What did you believe would happen if you protected it? Outcome: identify a chosen priority, distinguish an obligation from approval pressure, and make or rehearse a considered response.

lesson.title: What did your yes displace?
lesson.caption: One evening. A decision about where it goes.
lesson.notes: 2:00–3:00 worked scene. You have set aside Thursday evening to finish a portfolio. A friend asks for non-urgent help during that time. You want to keep the evening, but hear yourself preparing to agree. Saying yes and resenting the friend hides the choice. Attacking the friend for asking shifts responsibility. Name the concrete cost: the portfolio remains unfinished. Ask learners what their own last reluctant yes displaced. Do not imply every request should receive a no.

lesson.title:
Your life deserves
your investment
lesson.body:
You can choose where your effort goes.
You are responsible for the choice.
lesson.notes: 1:00–2:00 principle. We call this selfishness as a virtue: deliberate responsibility for your own flourishing. Freely chosen commitments and genuine responsibilities need attention. Other demands get accepted because we fear what refusing might make someone think. Learn to distinguish those cases. A request opens a decision. Courage to be disliked means allowing the possibility that a considered decision may disappoint someone.

lesson.title: The decision before the answer
rows: What have I already agreed to do?
What am I being asked to choose now?
What am I afraid they will think?
lesson.caption: An existing commitment needs honouring or renegotiation.
lesson.notes: 3:30–4:30 selection. Invite an ordinary situation with manageable consequences. Ask: have I already made a commitment? What would agreeing displace? If I were not trying to manage their opinion, what would I choose? There may be a good reason to agree. Make the reason explicit. A legitimate responsibility is different from approval pressure. If an existing promise cannot be kept, address it and renegotiate rather than pretending it never existed. Allow a sixty-second pause.

lesson.title: A clear response
lesson.quote:
“I can’t help on Thursday.
I’ve set that evening aside.”
lesson.caption: If pressed: “I’m keeping that time. Thursday won’t work for me.”
lesson.notes: 3:00–3:30 model, then rehearsal. Deliver the response calmly. It states availability without asking the friend to agree that the project matters. Offer another time only if genuinely willing and available. No invented excuse is necessary. If the friend asks whether the session can move, repeat the limit. The response does not guarantee the friend will be pleased. Use the course example as a model, not a compulsory script.

lesson.title: The rehearsal
rows: One real situation with manageable consequences
One or two sentences that state your answer
A reasonable follow-up and your response
lesson.caption: A considered yes, no or renegotiation can all show agency.
lesson.notes: 4:30–6:00. Read your response once. Remove invented excuses. Remove accusations that the person was wrong to ask. Check existing commitments. Imagine a reasonable follow-up and write what you would say. Pause for rehearsal. Guilt may appear. Record it as an experience, then examine whether you overlooked an actual responsibility. The feeling deserves attention but does not decide the issue. Use W01-D03 rather than adding a second assignment. Provide private rehearsal instead of mandatory public disclosure.

lesson.title: The field record
rows: What did I expect would happen?
What happened, or what did rehearsal reveal?
What did I do with the choice I made?
lesson.caption: Keep the record private where needed. A written account is enough.
lesson.notes: 6:00–7:00. Use the response in one appropriate situation. If none exists, rehearse with a partner or draft a response to a recent situation. Never manufacture conflict. Evidence is an honest account of a considered decision and response. Do not grade another person's approval. Check clarity, existing commitments, absence of invented excuses or accusations, and whether the learner actually invests in the protected priority. Assessment: demonstrated, revise or not yet evidenced. Do not require recordings or screenshots of others.

lesson.title:
What will you do
with the time
you protect?
lesson.body:
Tomorrow, recall the difference between
an obligation and approval pressure.
lesson.notes: 7:00–8:00. A clear boundary can make room for a skill, a piece of work or a life repeatedly postponed. What you protect must receive your effort. Ask for a specific next action for the named priority. Tomorrow, recall the distinction between an obligation and approval pressure without reopening the notes. Accept a deliberate yes supported by sound reasoning. Do not reward hostility or push participants into serious risk. This is educational practice, not treatment.
